cases.title: toMinorUnits of '19.99' at exponent 2 is 1999, not 1998
cases.notes: THE money bug. int(19.99 * 100) is 1998 in every IEEE-754 language: the nearest double to 19.99 is 19.98999999999999843..., and truncation takes the 1998. One cent, on every order.

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '0.07' at exponent 2 is 7
cases.notes: 0.07 * 100 is 7.000000000000001 as a double, so truncation gives 7 here by luck. The control row: an implementation that fixes 0001 by swapping trunc for round still passes this and still fails 0003.

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '8.615' at exponent 3 is 8615
cases.notes: 8.615 * 1000 is 8614.999999999999 as a double, so BOTH truncation and a naive round give 8614. The only way through is not to use a float at all. This is the row that forces exact decimal arithmetic rather than a rounding tweak.

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '1.005' at exponent 3 is 1005
cases.notes: KWD, BHD and JOD have three minor digits. A hard-coded 100 turns 1.005 dinars into 100 fils and undercharges by a factor of ten.

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '1000' at exponent 0 is 1000
cases.notes: JPY has no minor unit. A hard-coded 100 charges a hundred times the price.

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '-19.99' at exponent 2 is -1999
cases.notes: A refund line. abs(f(-x)) == abs(f(x)) is the property that matters for money, and it is the first thing to break when an implementation reaches for floor().

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '0.1' at exponent 2 is 10
cases.notes: Fewer decimals than the currency has: the value is scaled, not padded as text.

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '8.20' at exponent 2 is 820
cases.notes: A trailing zero is significant to a text parser and irrelevant to the value. 82 is what a strip-the-dot-and-parse implementation returns.

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '.5' at exponent 2 is 50
cases.notes: A leading dot is legal decimal notation and appears in hand-entered prices.

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '9007199254740.99' at exponent 2 is exact
cases.notes: Just under 2^53. Beyond this a JavaScript implementation needs BigInt; this row marks where the boundary is rather than crossing it, because a golden past it could not survive JSON.parse either.

cases.title: toMinorUnits of '007.50' at exponent 2 is 750
cases.notes: Must NOT be read as octal -- a trap in several languages' integer-parse routines.

cases.title: formatMinorUnits of 7 at exponent 2 is '0.07'
cases.notes: The commonest formatting bug: '0.7'. The fraction is zero-PADDED on the left to the currency's width, and the integer part is 0 rather than absent.

cases.title: formatMinorUnits of -7 at exponent 2 is '-0.07'
cases.notes: The sign belongs in front of the whole amount. Taking abs() to pad and forgetting to put it back gives '0.07'; applying it after the split gives '0.-07'.

cases.title: formatMinorUnits of 1000 at exponent 0 is '1000'
cases.notes: Exponent 0 means no decimal separator at all -- not '1000.' and not '1000.0'.

cases.title: formatMinorUnits inverts 0011 exactly
cases.notes: The inverse of 0011. Together they pin the round trip at the largest amount every runtime can still represent exactly.

cases.title: lineTotal of -1999 x 2 is -3998
cases.notes: A credit note is a negative line, and it must be the exact negation of the charge it reverses.

cases.title: lineTotal of 150000000 x 100000 is exact
cases.notes: 1.5e13 -- an ordinary invoice in a currency with no minor unit (IDR, VND). Well within a double, and a reminder that 'the numbers are small' is a USD assumption.
